b: As its title suggests, Maggie Kang and Chris Appelhans’s KPop Demon Hunters follows a K-pop girl group, HUNTR/X, whose members—Rumi (Arden Cho), Mira (May Hong), and Zoey (Yoo Ji-young)—defend humankind by keeping underworld demons at bay. Yet, surprisingly, what’s even less believable than that, and certainly less psychologically healthy, is the way these divas consistently put their fans’ safety and happiness above their own.

You might think a film about a pair of dueling pop groups—a burgeoning boy band of undercover demons called the Saja Boys eventually comes for HUNTR/X’s crown—would tackle the perils of stardom and fame. But the overstuffed yet undercooked script by Danya Jimenez, Hannah McMechan, Kang, and Appelhans never even touches on them. Instead, it merely pays lip service to any number of ideas, reducing them to self-help platitudes: sticking together, believing in yourself, finding your voice, and embracing your identity. Of course, these truisms are ultimately important only insofar as they allow the members of HUNTR/X to continue serving their fanbase unabated.

There’s no rest for the weary in pop stardom, and KPop Demon Hunters full-throatedly celebrates that by raising its trio of heroines to the level of literal superheroes who are worthy of blind allegiance and whose response to that allegiance must be to always give the fans what they want, when they want it. The film may not fully endorse toxic fandom, but it certainly suggests that corporate hegemony is a social net positive, in that the parasitic relationship between musicians and fans is not only insanely profitable but literally world-saving.

Fortunately, the film’s splashy colors, breakneck pacing, and upbeat musical numbers all help to distract from the hollowness and misguided nature of its messaging. Its integration of various animation styles is occasionally invigorating, and demons drawn from Korean folklore lend the proceedings a cultural specificity beyond the fluffy pop stylings. But KPop Demon Hunters is all too often reminiscent of the Saja Boys’s hit song “Soda Pop”: effervescent and vaguely engaging, but also full of empty calories and almost instantly forgettable.

The Criterion Collection’s disc features a new 4K master, approved by directors Maggie Kang and Chris Appelhans and presented in Dolby Vision HDR, that boasts immaculate image detail, ensuring that every texture and minuscule bit of visual design in this maximalist film stands out, whether in the characters’ elaborate costumes or the creatively designed mythical beings. The colors almost pop off the screen, particularly the vibrant pinks, purples, and blues, while even the subtlest variations in shading are clearly visible.

As strong as the image is, the real selling point here is the Dolby Atmos soundtrack, which not only gives the numerous songs a resounding power and depth, but features a perfectly balanced mix that lends clarity to all of the crowd noise, battle sounds, music, and dialogue while never allowing a single element to overwhelm the others.

This release includes the film’s feature-length animatic, along with a brief introduction by Kang and Appelhans, which offers an interesting peek at the storyboards used in the early visual design stage of KPop Demon Hunters. A new 49-minute documentary provides a wonderful overview of the entire artistic process behind the film and includes interviews with the directors and a slew of crew members who worked on everything from the art direction to the music editing and sound effects. There are also two videos by Tony Zhou and Taylor Ramos, the filmmakers behind the popular YouTube series Every Frame a Painting.

The first focuses on the film’s opening airplane fight sequence and consists mostly of interviews with crew members, while the second is a more traditional visual essay about the role that the songs and orchestral score play in the film. Lastly, there are seven lyric videos, the trailer, collectible postcards featuring original illustrations by artists who worked on the film, and a booklet featuring an essay by critic Karen Han that diligently contextualizes the popularity of KPop Demon Hunters within the two-decade rise of Korean pop culture on a global scale.
Criterion’s beautifully packaged release of Netflix’s surprise global hit features a spectacular A/V presentation and extras that attest to the massive undertaking of the film’s six-year production.

Cast: Arden Cho, EJAE, May Hong, Audrey Nuna, Yoo Ji-young, Rei Ami, Ahn Hyo-seop, Andrew Choi, Yunjin Kim, Ken Jeong, Lee Byung-hun, Daniel Dae Kim Director: Maggie Kang, Chris Appelhans Screenwriter: Danya Jimenez, Hannah McMechan, Maggie Kang, Chris Appelhans Distributor: The Criterion Collection Running Time: 96 min Rating: PG Year: 2025 Release Date: November 3, 2026 Buy: Video
